claim: Osteoclasts are unique in their capacity to degrade bone tissue.
source: Osteoclasts are unique in their capacity to degrade bone tissue.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of bone biology, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Osteoclasts form a specific structure called the sealing zone to achieve bone degradation.
source: To achieve this process, osteoclasts form a specific structure called the sealing zone, which creates a close contact with bone and confines the release of protons and hydrolases for bone degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the manuscript's introduction and references.

claim: The sealing zone creates a close contact with bone and confines the release of protons and hydrolases for bone degradation.
source: To achieve this process, osteoclasts form a specific structure called the sealing zone, which creates a close contact with bone and confines the release of protons and hydrolases for bone degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sealing zone function, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The sealing zone is composed of actin structures called podosomes nested in a dense actin network.
source: The sealing zone is composed of actin structures called podosomes nested in a dense actin network.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by prior literature and confirmed by the manuscript's observations.

claim: Random illumination microscopy allowed the identification and live imaging of densely packed actin cores within the sealing zone.
source: Random illumination microscopy allowed the identification and live imaging of densely packed actin cores within the sealing zone.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Actin cores within the sealing zone are locally synchronized based on cross-correlation analysis of actin content fluctuations.
source: A cross-correlation analysis of the fluctuations of actin content at these cores indicates that they are locally synchronized.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The sealing zone is composed of groups of synchronized cores linked by α-actinin1 positive filaments and encircled by adhesion complexes.
source: Further examination shows that the sealing zone is composed of groups of synchronized cores linked by α-actinin1 positive filaments, and encircled by adhesion complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on super-resolution imaging and analysis of protein distributions presented in the manuscript.

claim: The confinement of bone degradation mediators is achieved through the coordination of islets of actin cores rather than global coordination of all podosomal subunits.
source: Thus, we propose that the confinement of bone degradation mediators is achieved through the coordination of islets of actin cores and not by the global coordination of all podosomal subunits forming the sealing zone.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Protons accumulate into the resorption lacuna thanks to the vacuolar H+-ATPase (v-ATPase), lowering the local pH and facilitating the solubilization of apatite.
source: To do so, protons accumulate into the resorption lacuna thanks to the vacuolar H+-ATPase (v-ATPase), thus lowering the local pH and facilitating the solubilization of apatite, the main mineral component of bone.
evidence: This is established knowledge about osteoclast bone resorption mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Apatite is the main mineral component of bone.
source: To do so, protons accumulate into the resorption lacuna thanks to the vacuolar H+-ATPase (v-ATPase), thus lowering the local pH and facilitating the solubilization of apatite, the main mineral component of bone.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bone composition.

claim: The acidic environment in the resorption lacuna enhances the digestion of bone organic matrix by proteases such as cathepsin K.
source: This acidic environment is also prone to enhance the digestion of bone organic matrix by proteases secreted by osteoclasts such as cathepsin K (Teitelbaum, 2007; Soysa and Alles, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: The efficiency of bone resorption relies on the ability of the cell to create an enclosed resorption compartment via the formation of the sealing zone.
source: The efficiency of this process relies on the ability of the cell to create an enclosed resorption compartment, via the formation of a unique cytoskeletal structure, the sealing zone (Jurdic et al., 2006; Delaisse et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: The sealing zone was first described as a subcellular entity made of electron dense material and apparently deprived of any organelle, resulting in the first denomination as the 'clear zone'.
source: First described as a subcellular entity made of electron dense material and apparently deprived of any organelle, thus resulting in first denomination as the 'clear zone', the sealing zone was then revealed to consist in a dense accumulation of actin filaments forming a circular shape surrounding the resorption lacuna (Zambonin-Zallone et al., 1988; Kanehisa et al., 1990; Teti et al., 1991; King and Holtrop, 1975; Han et al., 2019).
evidence: This is historical information about the sealing zone supported by citations.

claim: The sealing zone consists of a dense accumulation of actin filaments forming a circular shape surrounding the resorption lacuna.
source: First described as a subcellular entity made of electron dense material and apparently deprived of any organelle, thus resulting in first denomination as the 'clear zone', the sealing zone was then revealed to consist in a dense accumulation of actin filaments forming a circular shape surrounding the resorption lacuna (Zambonin-Zallone et al., 1988; Kanehisa et al., 1990; Teti et al., 1991; King and Holtrop, 1975; Han et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Scanning electron microscopy examination of cells removed of their basal membrane revealed the peculiar arrangement of actin filaments within the sealing zone and unveiled the existence of a dense network of podosomes composing this structure.
source: Examination with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of cells removed of their basal membrane brought to light the peculiar arrangement of actin filaments within this structure, and particularly unveiled the existence of a dense network of podosomes composing this structure (Luxenburg et al., 2007; Akisaka and Yoshida, 2015; Akisaka and Yoshida, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Podosomes are adhesion structures that are generally scattered in macrophages and dendritic cells.
source: Podosomes are adhesion structures that are generally scattered in macrophages and dendritic cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about podosome distribution in different cell types.

claim: Podosome typical components such as vinculin, paxillin, talin, and cortactin are localized in the sealing zone.
source: Podosome typical components, such as vinculin, paxillin, talin, or cortactin, are also localized in the sealing zone (Chabadel et al., 2007; Saltel et al., 2008; Lakkakorpi et al., 1993; Lakkakorpi et al., 2001; Pfaff and Jurdic, 2001; Hurst et al., 2003; Gil-Henn et al., 2007; Ory et al., 2008; Ma et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Vinculin, paxillin, and talin form a 'double circle' flanking the sealing zone on each side, while cortactin mainly colocalizes with actin in between.
source: In a distinct way compared to single podosomes, vinculin, paxillin, and talin were reported to form a 'double circle' flanking the sealing zone on each side, while cortactin mainly colocalized with actin in between (Jurdic et al., 2006; Lakkakorpi et al., 1993; Pfaff and Jurdic, 2001; Lakkakorpi et al., 1999; Lakkakorpi and Väänänen, 1996; Tehrani et al., 2006).
evidence: This is previously reported knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Most studies on the bone degradation machinery were carried out on osteoclasts on glass substrates instead of bone due to the lack of optical transparency and high auto-fluorescence of the mineralized matrix.
source: Noteworthy, most of the studies on the bone degradation machinery were carried out based on observations of osteoclasts on glass substrates instead of bone, due to the lack of optical transparency and high auto-fluorescence of the mineralized matrix.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous studies, based on knowledge of the field.

claim: Actin structures on bone differ from those formed on glass, mainly in their total width and the interconnectivity and density of actin cores.
source: Indeed, it has been suggested that actin structures on bone differ from the ones formed on glass, mainly in their total width, and the interconnectivity and density of actin cores within (Luxenburg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is previously suggested knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Only structures formed on bone or bone-mimicking materials are called sealing zone, while structures on glass are denominated as 'sealing zone like' or podosome belts.
source: Therefore, only structures formed on bone or bone-mimicking materials are called sealing zone, structures on glass being denominated as 'sealing zone like' or podosome belts (Jurdic et al., 2006; Saltel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a nomenclature convention in the field supported by the cited references.

claim: Podosome belts on glass share certain characteristics with sealing zones, including areas where podosome cores appear fused.
source: On glass, osteoclasts form structures called podosome belts, sharing certain characteristics with sealing zones (Jurdic et al., 2006). In particular, podosome belts also exhibit areas where podosome cores appear fused, that is when sets of several cores are brought together inside a single and large ring of adhesion sites, similar to the described structure of the sealing zone.
evidence: This is a comparison based on established knowledge and observations in the manuscript.

claim: Fusion of podosome cores was observed in 9.4+/-3.5% of multinucleated human osteoclasts on glass.
source: Indeed, this fusion of podosome cores was observed in 9.4+/-3.5% of multinucleated human osteoclasts.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the manuscript's experimental data.

claim: Cortactin in-plane distribution is characterized by an accumulation in the first 250 nm surrounding the actin cores.
source: Cortactin in-plane distribution was characterized by an accumulation in the first 250 nm surrounding the actin cores, and kept at a rather constant height of approximately 164 nm while actin height peaked at the core and then decreased by approximately 50 nm on both sides (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: This is a finding from DONALD super-resolution imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cortactin is kept at a rather constant height of approximately 164 nm.
source: Cortactin in-plane distribution was characterized by an accumulation in the first 250 nm surrounding the actin cores, and kept at a rather constant height of approximately 164 nm while actin height peaked at the core and then decreased by approximately 50 nm on both sides (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DONALD imaging data.

claim: Actin height peaks at the core and then decreases by approximately 50 nm on both sides.
source: Cortactin in-plane distribution was characterized by an accumulation in the first 250 nm surrounding the actin cores, and kept at a rather constant height of approximately 164 nm while actin height peaked at the core and then decreased by approximately 50 nm on both sides (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DONALD imaging data.

claim: α-actinin1 is preferentially localized in the vicinity of the actin cores, up to 500 nm in distance.
source: α-actinin1 was preferentially localized in the vicinity of the actin cores, up to 500 nm in distance.
evidence: This is a finding from DONALD imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: α-actinin1 height stays approximately constant at approximately 126 nm throughout the distance profile.
source: Similarly to cortactin, its height stayed approximately constant throughout the distance profile, at approximately 126 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DONALD imaging data.

claim: Vinculin, paxillin, talin, and filamin A are mostly absent from the regions of dense actin staining and encircle multiple actin cores.
source: Vinculin, paxillin, talin, and filamin A were mostly absent from the regions of dense actin staining, and encircled multiple actin cores (Figure 1A–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2G-J).
evidence: This is a finding from DONALD imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vinculin and talin-C heights decline by nearly 20 nm toward the inner part of the cell.
source: Vinculin and talin-C heights declined by nearly 20 nm toward the inner part of the cell (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DONALD imaging data.

claim: Filamin A average height is 45 nm and exhibits almost no change in height when away from the belt center.
source: In contrast, filamin A and paxillin, for which average heights were 45 nm and 139 nm, respectively, exhibited almost no change in height when away from the belt center (Figure 1H–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2G-J).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DONALD imaging data.

claim: Paxillin average height is 139 nm and exhibits almost no change in height when away from the belt center.
source: In contrast, filamin A and paxillin, for which average heights were 45 nm and 139 nm, respectively, exhibited almost no change in height when away from the belt center (Figure 1H–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2G-J).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DONALD imaging data.

claim: There is little difference in terms of organization between the internal and external distributions of the different podosome components analyzed.
source: Of note, our analyses revealed little difference in terms of organization between the internal and external distributions of the different podosome components analyzed, the most striking being a closer proximity of the vinculin to the cores on the outer side of the belt, suggesting that the podosome belt is overall a symmetric structure.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of DONALD imaging data.

claim: Vinculin is in closer proximity to the cores on the outer side of the belt.
source: Of note, our analyses revealed little difference in terms of organization between the internal and external distributions of the different podosome components analyzed, the most striking being a closer proximity of the vinculin to the cores on the outer side of the belt, suggesting that the podosome belt is overall a symmetric structure.
evidence: This is a finding from DONALD imaging data analysis.

claim: The podosome belt is overall a symmetric structure.
source: Of note, our analyses revealed little difference in terms of organization between the internal and external distributions of the different podosome components analyzed, the most striking being a closer proximity of the vinculin to the cores on the outer side of the belt, suggesting that the podosome belt is overall a symmetric structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of DONALD imaging data.

claim: Human osteoclasts efficiently degraded bone after 3 days on bovine bone slices, as shown by scanning electron microscopy observations.
source: After 3 days, osteoclasts efficiently degraded bone, as shown by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from SEM imaging presented in the manuscript.

claim: SEM acquisitions of unroofed cells confirmed that the sealing zones formed by human osteoclasts are composed of individual F-actin cores.
source: SEM acquisitions of unroofed cells confirmed that the sealing zones formed by human osteoclasts are composed of individual F-actin cores (Figure 2B), similarly to what was shown in osteoclasts differentiated from the mouse cell line RAW 264.7 or harvested from rabbit long bones (Luxenburg et al., 2007; Akisaka and Yoshida, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from SEM imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Actin cores in the sealing zone are nested in a dense network of actin filaments and appear connected to their neighbors by filaments running parallel to the substrate.
source: These cores were nested in a dense network of actin filaments, and appeared connected to their neighbors by filaments running parallel to the substrate (Figure 2B', arrowheads).
evidence: This is an observation from SEM imaging presented in the manuscript.

claim: Analysis of 457 cores in nine different cells yielded a median core radius of 114 nm by SEM.
source: Analysis of 457 cores in nine different cells yielded a median core radius of 114 nm (Figure 2D), that is two times smaller than the radius of macrophage podosomes (Proag et al., 2015; Jasnin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from SEM image analysis.

claim: The median core radius of 114 nm in osteoclast sealing zones is two times smaller than the radius of macrophage podosomes.
source: Analysis of 457 cores in nine different cells yielded a median core radius of 114 nm (Figure 2D), that is two times smaller than the radius of macrophage podosomes (Proag et al., 2015; Jasnin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the manuscript's data and cited references.

claim: Direct neighbor pairs in the sealing zone are 705 nm apart by SEM analysis.
source: Direct neighbor pairs were 705 nm apart (Figure 2E), and first neighbors were 443 nm apart (Figure 2F), similarly to what was described previously (Deguchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from SEM image analysis using Delaunay's tessellation.

claim: First neighbors in the sealing zone are 443 nm apart by SEM analysis.
source: Direct neighbor pairs were 705 nm apart (Figure 2E), and first neighbors were 443 nm apart (Figure 2F), similarly to what was described previously (Deguchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from SEM image analysis using Delaunay's tessellation.

claim: RIM efficiently allows for the observation of single actin cores within the sealing zones of human osteoclasts.
source: As the distribution of radii and neighbor distances were similar with SEM and RIM, we concluded that RIM efficiently allows for the observation of single actin cores within the sealing zones of human osteoclasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of SEM and RIM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RIM imaging of the sealing zone shows an average core radius of 97 nm.
source: The radius distribution yielded an average value of 97 nm (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RIM image analysis.

claim: By RIM analysis, direct neighbors in the sealing zone are in a 694 nm distance range.
source: Direct neighbors were in a 694 nm distance range (Figure 2E), with first neighbors being 399 nm apart (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RIM image analysis using Delaunay's tessellation.

claim: By RIM analysis, first neighbors in the sealing zone are 399 nm apart.
source: Direct neighbors were in a 694 nm distance range (Figure 2E), with first neighbors being 399 nm apart (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RIM image analysis using Delaunay's tessellation.

claim: Actin cores in the sealing zone appear stable over at least 30 min based on widefield fluorescence microscopy observations.
source: Subsequent deconvolution of the images and color-coding for time using a rainbow scale revealed that cores appeared stable over at least 30 min and analysis of kymographs along the sealing zone revealed actin intensity oscillations during the entire duration of the acquisitions (Figure 3A, Video 2).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse widefield microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Analysis of kymographs along the sealing zone revealed actin intensity oscillations during the entire duration of the acquisitions.
source: Subsequent deconvolution of the images and color-coding for time using a rainbow scale revealed that cores appeared stable over at least 30 min and analysis of kymographs along the sealing zone revealed actin intensity oscillations during the entire duration of the acquisitions (Figure 3A, Video 2).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse widefield microscopy data analysis.

claim: Variations of the actin content in podosome cores fluctuate synchronously between neighbors.
source: Variations of the actin content in podosome cores were measured and appeared to fluctuate synchronously between neighbors (Figure 3B and Video 3, left).
evidence: This is a finding from RIM time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Highest Pearson coefficient values between 1 and 0.37 were obtained for cores within a 700 nm radius distance.
source: Highest Pearson coefficient values between 1 and 0.37, corresponding to half of the maximum mean value, were obtained for cores within a 700 nm radius distance.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from cross-correlation analysis of time-lapse RIM data.

claim: Pearson coefficients slowly decrease to approximately 0.10 at longer distances beyond 700 nm.
source: They slowly decreased to approximately 0.10 at longer distances (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from cross-correlation analysis of time-lapse RIM data.

claim: There is a spatial synchrony between neighbors within the sealing zone, comparable to observations for podosomes in human macrophages.
source: This result hinted at the existence of a spatial synchrony between neighbors within the sealing zone, comparable to observations for podosomes in human macrophages (Proag et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the manuscript's data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Three specific frequencies prevail in actin content fluctuations: 0.01 Hz, 0.04 Hz, and 0.15 Hz, corresponding to periods of approximately 100 s, 25 s, and 7 s, respectively.
source: Moreover, potential periodicity of actin content fluctuations was examined through analysis of the Fourier spectra corresponding to live acquisitions. This yielded three specific frequencies that seemed to prevail: 0.01 Hz, 0.04 Hz, and 0.15 Hz, corresponding to periods of approximately 100 s, 25 s, and 7 s, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from Fourier analysis of time-lapse RIM data.

claim: Similar oscillation periods had previously been identified in macrophages by examining the stiffness variations of single podosomes.
source: In macrophages, similar oscillation periods had previously been identified by examining the stiffness variations of single podosomes (Labernadie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published work supported by the citation.

claim: Polymerization and depolymerization regions in the sealing zone appear as clusters with slowly varying areas, containing a few actin cores.
source: Strikingly, polymerization and depolymerization regions appeared as clusters with slowly varying areas, containing a few actin cores (Figure 3D, Video 3, right).
evidence: This is a finding from differential film analysis of time-lapse RIM data.

claim: Actin polymerization and depolymerization processes appear to be synchronous within actin core clusters.
source: Actin polymerization and depolymerization processes thus appeared to be synchronous within actin core clusters.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of time-lapse RIM data.

claim: There is a local synchrony of F-actin oscillations between cores of the same superstructure.
source: In conclusion, we showed a local synchrony of F-actin oscillations between cores of the same superstructure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the time-lapse RIM data analysis.

claim: The local synchrony of actin cores suggests the organization of actin cores into functional clusters within the sealing zone.
source: This suggests the organization of actin cores into functional clusters within the sealing zone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synchrony data.

claim: Cortactin is localized within the core domain and displays a wider distribution compared to the average core diameter.
source: Cortactin was localized within the core domain, as had been previously reported (Hurst et al., 2003), and displayed a wider distribution compared to the average core diameter (Figure 4A and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from RIM imaging of fixed samples on bone.

claim: α-actinin1 mostly colocalizes with actin at the close periphery of the core and appears less present in the most central part of the core.
source: α-actinin1 mostly colocalized with actin at the close periphery of the core, and appeared less present in the most central part of the core (Figure 4B and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from RIM imaging of fixed samples on bone.

claim: Filamin A, vinculin, paxillin and talin preferentially encircle multiple actin cores, with little staining in between cores in the inner part of the sealing zone.
source: Filamin A, vinculin, paxillin and talin were preferentially encircling multiple actin cores, with little staining in between cores in the inner part of the sealing zone (Figure 4C–D and E, Figure 4—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is a finding from RIM imaging of fixed samples on bone.

claim: Islets of clustered cores in the sealing zone are 2.3+/-2.1 µm² (average +/-SD) in size.
source: Measurements of these islets of clustered cores showed that they were 2.3+/-2.1 µm² (average +/-SD) and contained 7+/-8 (average +/-SD) cores.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RIM image analysis.

claim: Islets of clustered cores in the sealing zone contain 7+/-8 (average +/-SD) cores.
source: Measurements of these islets of clustered cores showed that they were 2.3+/-2.1 µm² (average +/-SD) and contained 7+/-8 (average +/-SD) cores.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RIM image analysis.

claim: The sealing zone is composed of islets of actin cores that are bordered by a network of adhesion complexes.
source: These observations showed a strong divergence with the 'double circle' distribution described before (Lakkakorpi et al., 1993; Lakkakorpi and Väänänen, 1996), as the sealing zone appeared to be composed of islets of actin cores that are bordered by a network of adhesion complexes.
evidence: This is a finding from RIM imaging that contrasts with previous models.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the actin content and each of the podosome components cortactin, α-actinin1, filamin A, vinculin, paxillin and talin.
source: These analyses revealed a positive correlation between the actin content and each of the podosome components (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis of RIM images.

claim: Time-lapse RIM imaging of both F-actin and paxillin confirmed that paxillin intensity fluctuations are locally correlated with F-actin intensity.
source: Time-lapse RIM imaging of both F-actin and paxillin further confirmed that paxillin intensity fluctuations are locally correlated with F-actin intensity (Figure 5B–C, Video 4).
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse RIM imaging of live cells.

claim: There is a local regulation between polymerization of actin in the core and accumulation of adhesion complex proteins.
source: These results suggested that, in addition to the local core coordination, there was also a local regulation between polymerization of actin in the core and accumulation of adhesion complex proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation data from RIM imaging.

claim: Actin cores localized within the same islets are synchronized with each other and with the surrounding adhesion complexes.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrated that the actin cores which were localized within the same islets were synchronized with each other and with the surrounding adhesion complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the time-lapse RIM imaging data.

claim: The study provides a nanoscale picture of the architecture, spatial organization and dynamics of podosomes in the sealing zone of human osteoclasts adhering on bone.
source: This study provides a nanoscale picture of the architecture, spatial organization and dynamics of podosomes in the sealing zone of human osteoclasts adhering on bone.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contributions.

claim: The 3D localization of major actin crosslinkers inside the podosome belt and examination of their axial localization hints at the possible existence of tension within the integrin adhesion sites.
source: First, we gave a detailed insight into the inner organization of the sealing zone with the 3D localization of major actin crosslinkers inside the podosome belt, and examination of their axial localization hinted at the possible existence of tension within the integrin adhesion sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DONALD imaging data.

claim: Podosome cores in the sealing zone are within the submicron range from their direct neighbors.
source: Second, using RIM, we showed that podosome cores were within the submicron range from their direct neighbors.
evidence: This is a finding from RIM imaging data.

claim: Actin cores in the sealing zone display long-term spatial stability during bone resorption.
source: Third, by monitoring podosomes in the sealing zone by time-lapse super-resolution microscopy, we characterized the long-term spatial stability of actin cores during bone resorption and we revealed a synchronous behavior for actin cores within a distance of 1 µm.
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse RIM imaging data.

claim: Actin cores within a distance of 1 µm display synchronous behavior.
source: Third, by monitoring podosomes in the sealing zone by time-lapse super-resolution microscopy, we characterized the long-term spatial stability of actin cores during bone resorption and we revealed a synchronous behavior for actin cores within a distance of 1 µm.
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse RIM imaging data.

claim: Actin fluctuations in the sealing zone are probably the result of the constant renewal of the actin network, with a likely treadmilling of actin filaments from the plasma membrane towards the apical part of the cell.
source: These fluctuations are probably the result of the constant renewal of the actin network in the sealing zone (Saltel et al., 2004), with a likely treadmilling of actin filaments from the plasma membrane towards the apical part of the cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed fluctuations and cited literature.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex and cortactin are central in the dynamics of the sealing zone and play a key role in its function, probably via the generation of a protrusion force applied to the bone substrate.
source: The Arp2/3 complex and cortactin are central in these dynamics (Hurst et al., 2003), and play a key role in the function of the sealing zone, probably via the generation of a protrusion force applied to the bone substrate, similarly to what was shown for macrophage podosomes (Bouissou et al., 2017; Proag et al., 2015; Labernadie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the manuscript's findings and comparison with cited literature on macrophage podosomes.

claim: Synchronous neighbors in the sealing zone are grouped within clusters, which correspond to islets surrounded by adhesion complexes composed of vinculin, talin, paxillin and filamin A.
source: Finally, we found that synchronous neighbors were grouped within clusters, which corresponded to islets surrounded by adhesion complexes composed of vinculin, talin, paxillin and filamin A.
evidence: This is a finding from RIM imaging and analysis.

claim: Vinculin and talin-C appear to rise when situated closer to the actin cores, which could be the first insight into the identification of possible tension within the podosome belt.
source: Moreover, vinculin and talin-C appeared to rise when situated closer to the actin cores. This interesting finding could be the first insight into the identification of possible tension within the podosome belt.
evidence: This is an inference based on DONALD imaging data.

claim: When talin is stretched in podosome rings of macrophages, vinculin height is higher, probably because vinculin binding sites appear when talin acquires an extended conformation.
source: In fact, in podosome rings of macrophages, it was observed that when talin is stretched, vinculin height is higher, probably because vinculin binding sites are appearing when talin acquires an extended conformation (Bouissou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is knowledge from cited literature used to interpret the manuscript's findings.

claim: Cortactin, α-actinin1 and filamin A are mainly localized around 150 nm above the plasma membrane, with a dislocated distribution compared to actin.
source: In addition, cortactin, α-actinin1 and filamin A were mainly localized around 150 nm above the plasma membrane, with a dislocated distribution compared to actin.
evidence: This is a finding from DONALD imaging data.

claim: There exist different sets of actin filaments within the sealing zone: those enriched in cross-linkers in an upper layer and those devoid of cross-linkers near the plasma membrane.
source: This suggests the existence of different sets of actin filaments within the sealing zone, those enriched in cross-linkers in an upper layer and those devoid of cross-linkers near the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DONALD imaging data showing different protein distributions.

claim: Within podosome islets, different populations of actin filaments (actin cores positive for cortactin and lateral filaments positive for actinin or filamin-A) coexist and are probably mechanically coupled and coordinated to allow force generation and efficient sealing.
source: The present manuscript also suggests that, within podosome islets, different populations of actin filaments (actin cores positive for cortactin and lateral filaments positive for actinin or filamin-A) coexist (Figure 6) and are probably mechanically coupled and coordinated to allow force generation and efficient sealing of the bone breakdown zone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the manuscript's imaging data.

claim: The difference between the 'double circle' distribution and the islet organization observed in this study probably stems from the better resolution of the images and from the fact that most previous studies were performed on mouse osteoclasts rather than human osteoclasts.
source: This difference probably stems not only from the better resolution of the images presented in this manuscript but also from the fact that most of the studies on the organization of sealing zones were performed on mouse osteoclasts (Jurdic et al., 2006; Saltel et al., 2008, Lakkakorpi et al., 2001, Ma et al., 2010; Lakkakorpi et al., 1999; Lakkakorpi and Väänänen, 1996), and not on human osteoclasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the manuscript's findings with previous literature.

claim: Local oscillations associated with actin remodeling within the cores were revealed and characterized for the first time in the sealing zone.
source: Here, local oscillations associated with actin remodeling within the cores were revealed and characterized for the first time in the sealing zone.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the manuscript's findings.

claim: The actin oscillations observed in the sealing zone have a time periodicity of approximately 100 s, which is much slower than the actin oscillations observed in scattered macrophage podosomes.
source: Actin signal processing yielded a time periodicity for these oscillations of approximately 100 s, which is much slower than the actin oscillations observed in scattered macrophage podosomes (Bouissou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from Fourier analysis of time-lapse data, compared with cited literature.

claim: Oscillations in macrophage podosomes depend on myosin IIA activity.
source: It was previously shown that these oscillations in macrophage podosomes depend on myosin IIA activity (Labernadie et al., 2014; van den Dries et al., 2013).
evidence: This is knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Cross-correlation analysis between signals associated with two cores in the same cell revealed the existence of a spatial synchrony between neighbors up to an approximate 2 µm distance scale.
